analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal handgun licensing and registration system and bans assault weapons, cheap handguns, and large magazines.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 6 Senate cosponsors, the Gun Violence Prevention Act of 1994 died in the Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a nationwide handgun licensing and registration system run by the states, required a safety course before buying a handgun, and banned semiautomatic assault weapons, cheap "Saturday night special" handguns, magazines holding more than six rounds, silencers, and short-barreled guns. It would also have limited buyers to one handgun per 30 days, required a $300 license to own more than 20 firearms, raised gun dealer license fees from as little as $10 to as much as $10,000, and given shooting victims a new right to sue sellers who broke federal gun laws. It never reached a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been people exposed to gun violence — families, children, and communities — through a background-checked, fingerprint-based handgun license in every state, a required safety course, a 7-day waiting period, child-storage rules, and bans on the cheapest easily-concealed handguns and military-style weapons. Police would have gained registration records to trace guns used in crimes, and victims shot with guns transferred illegally could have sued the seller for damages, with lawyers' fees awarded to winners. States would have received startup grants, authorized at $200 million a year, to build the licensing systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence; crime victims

how_it_helps.text: Requires every handgun buyer to obtain a state license issued only after a fingerprint-based background check, proof of residency, a two-hour safety course, and a passed exam, and creates a registration form for each handgun transfer so police can trace guns used in crimes.

Bans the manufacture, transfer, and possession of semiautomatic assault weapons, 'Saturday night special' handguns, silencers, short-barreled shotguns and rifles, and ammunition magazines holding more than six rounds, with a 7-day waiting period before any handgun transfer.

Bars gun transfers to people convicted of violent crimes or under court protection orders, raises the minimum age to 21 for handgun possession, makes it a federal crime to leave a loaded gun where a child under 16 can reach it, and requires new guns to be child-resistant.

Gives shooting victims a federal right to sue anyone who transferred a gun or ammunition in violation of law, with costs and attorneys' fees for prevailing plaintiffs and punitive damages for reckless violations, and requires gun dealers to carry $100,000 in liability insurance.

Cracks down on sellers by raising license fees from $10-$200 to $1,000-$10,000, allowing three inspections a year instead of one, requiring 24-hour theft reports, licensing ammunition dealers, and barring sales from vehicles or unlicensed locations.

analysis.who_pays: The costs would have fallen on the firearms industry and on gun owners. Manufacturers would have lost entire product lines (assault weapons, Saturday night specials, large-capacity magazines, non-childproof guns). Dealers would have paid new fees up to fifty times higher, faced tripled inspections, needed liability insurance, and been barred from selling at gun shows or from vehicles. Individual buyers would have paid license, course, and registration fees, waited 7 days, and been limited to one handgun per 30 days. States would have had to build licensing and registration systems, with federal money covering only startup costs and only if Congress appropriated it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, owners, and state agencies

drawbacks.text: Law-abiding gun owners would have faced significant new burdens: a state license, safety course and fees, a 7-day waiting period, a one-handgun-per-30-days limit, and a $300 three-year 'arsenal license' just to own more than 20 firearms or 1,000 rounds of ammunition.

The licensing and registration burden would have landed on states, which must issue, track, and revoke licenses and register every handgun transfer; the $200 million in authorized startup grants covers only initial costs and depends on future appropriations.

Raising dealer license fees to $1,000-$10,000 a year (from as low as $10, with renewals jumping from $90 to $1,000 a year) would likely have pushed small and part-time dealers out of business, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety gains — background-checked licensing, registration for tracing, and bans on the cheapest concealable handguns and military-style weapons — were potentially large, but the bill was drafted so broadly that its costs fell heavily on ordinary gun owners as well as the industry, not just on criminals. The arsenal license, one-gun-a-month rule, and fifty-fold fee increases went well beyond the narrower measures Congress actually passed in the same period (the Brady background-check waiting period and the 1994 assault weapons ban), which is a major reason it attracted only 6 cosponsors and died without debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in March 1994, and then sat there with no committee vote and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on March 1, 1994 with five Democratic colleagues and one Republican, John Chafee of Rhode Island, as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced.
The Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution held a hearing on March 23, 1994 and received the referral two days later, but the full committee never voted on the bill.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 103rd Congress; the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1995, without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and owners were better off: no federal licensing, registration, waiting period, one-gun-a-month limit, arsenal license, or product bans ever took effect from this bill. Supporters of broad gun regulation gained nothing from it, though narrower measures — the Brady Act background check and the 1994 assault weapons ban — became law separately.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor with introductory remarks.

for.name: Sens. Edward Kennedy, Bill Bradley, Frank Lautenberg, Barbara Boxer, and Claiborne Pell
Sen. John Chafee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only Republican among its six supporters.

against.name: Sen. Joseph Biden
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill to a subcommittee, held one hearing, and never reported it out or scheduled a committee vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against the bill, which opponents labeled 'Brady II,' framing it as a back-door national gun registration scheme.

sides.party_line_note: Five of the six cosponsors were Democrats and the only Republican was moderate John Chafee; because no vote was ever held, no record exists of where the rest of the Senate stood.

industries.note: The bill would have banned several of their product lines outright — semiautomatic assault weapons, 'Saturday night special' handguns, magazines over six rounds, silencers — and required childproofing on all new guns. The industry's interest in keeping those products on the market ran directly against the bill's public-safety purpose.

License fees would have jumped from $10-$200 to $1,000-$10,000, with annual renewals rising from $90 to $1,000; dealers would have faced three inspections a year, mandatory $100,000 liability insurance, 24-hour theft reporting, and a ban on sales from vehicles or unlicensed locations. Smaller dealers would have been squeezed hardest.

Every gun dealer would have had to buy a new $100,000 personal-injury liability policy, creating a mandated market for insurers. The same coverage would have compensated people injured by negligently sold handguns.

Selling handgun ammunition would have required a federal dealer license and buyer license verification for the first time, adding licensing and recordkeeping costs to a previously lightly regulated trade.
